answer.rationale: Rollback (memory_b1) is off the table: compliance has ruled the security patch non-revertible, so the strongest inherited precedent is unusable regardless of how well it worked on day 18. That leaves the degradation's one hard signal — it is confined to the primary region and on the write path — which points at regional failover (memory_b2) as the only candidate that addresses the fault domain directly rather than shaving load at the margins. Add_capacity (memory_b3) worked as pre-provisioned headroom before a known peak, not as a mid-incident action 90 minutes into a climb; circuit breakers (memory_b4) contained an external partner failure, whereas this looks internal and would fail settlement writes fast rather than preserve them; route_read_replicas (memory_b5) is the lowest-risk option and would help if read contention from dashboards is inflating write latency, so I want its source record to see whether the day-55 case actually resembled a write-path saturation or merely a reporting-load problem. I am verifying memory_b2 specifically to learn the conditions of the March cutover: whether it happened under heavy write load at peak and whether any in-flight writes were lost or reconciled, because 'traffic shifted cleanly, error rates recovered in minutes' is an availability claim and is silent on write durability — which is exactly the constraint that dominates here at settlement peak. That gap matters because every inherited memory is an outcome-only success record with no base rate, no failure cases, and no record of conditions that differed; treating them as generalizable rules is survivorship bias, and a full cutover justified on that basis is precisely how a partial-information decision hardens into an unrecoverable one. So I intend failover at the smallest guarded scale: shift a thin slice of write traffic to the secondary with reconciliation checks and an explicit abort, which tests the region-confinement hypothesis while keeping the bulk of settlement writes on a path whose durability I already understand. If memory_b2 reveals write loss or a read-only failover, or if memory_b5 shows a genuinely analogous write-saturation case, I will switch to replica routing instead. I am not yet confident which mechanism is causal, and the one-intervention limit makes an irreversible bet on an unverified precedent the worst available trade.
